title: Constellation Acquires SpikedAde for $75 Million as Boozy Sports Drink Segment Booms
summary:
On Tuesday Constellation Brands announced its acquisition of SpikedAde, one of the leading ready-to-drink (RTD) beverages in the growing boozy sports drink segment. Constellation agreed to a payment of $75 million for 100 percent ownership of the fast-growing brand, though payments in the next five years could reach up to an additional $278 million contingent on performance. The acquisition marks Constellation Brands’s first foray into hard sports drinks — a growing segment within the already expanding category of spirit-based ready-to-drink beverages.

The article Constellation Acquires SpikedAde for $75 Million as Boozy Sports Drink Segment Booms appeared first on VinePair.
content:
On Tuesday Constellation Brands announced its acquisition of SpikedAde, one of the leading ready-to-drink (RTD) beverages in the growing boozy sports drink segment. Constellation agreed to a payment of $75 million for 100 percent ownership of the fast-growing brand, though payments in the next five years could reach up to an additional $278 million contingent on performance.

The acquisition marks Constellation Brands’s first foray into hard sports drinks — a growing segment within the already expanding category of spirit-based ready-to-drink beverages. SpikedAde is the runner-up to “Ade” segment leader Super Lyte, which boasts 65 percent share of off-premise sales, according to Brewbound.

Chief executive officer Jason Cohen founded SpikedAde in New Jersey in 2025. It packages non-carbonated, vodka-based drinks with Gatorade-like flavors, such as Electric Orange and Electric Blue, into 12-ounce cans. Cohen claimed he raised $10 million in the first two weeks of this year alone to expand the brand outside of New Jersey.

Now, SpikedAde is ranked among the top 25 RTD brands, according to NielsenIQ data. And though SpikeAde’s presence now extends along the East Coast, Constellation’s pickup will bring the brand to markets nationwide.

“With Constellation’s scale and expertise behind it, we’re excited to see SpikedAde reach even more consumers with its distinctive positioning and continue its remarkable growth trajectory,” Cohen states in a press release issued by Constellation.

The “Ade” category has exploded this past year. With Super Lyte, SpikedAde, and Vodkade leading the charge, the segment burst past the one million case mark this year, according to NielsenIQ data. With better-for-you and health-conscious trends swarming the market, new and established alcohol brands are leaning into sports marketing and functional ingredients like protein and electrolytes. And SpikedAde fits the bill, touting a zero-sugar, 100-calorie liquid.

“As consumer preferences evolve and new occasions continue to emerge, we’re excited to build on the strong foundation the SpikedAde team has created,” Constellation president and CEO Nicholas Fink says in the release.

title: New NYC Bar Under Fire for Copying Name and Branding of World’s Best Bar
summary:
As the global cohort of bartenders and industry enthusiasts gears up for this year’s announcement of the World’s 50 Best Bars tomorrow, last year’s victor Bar Leone in Hong Kong is soaking in its time at the top spot. And as it awaits this year’s ranking, the team at Bar Leone faces a less-expected obstacle: a new bar with the same name and near-identical branding that opened last month in New York City. Rome native Lorenzo Antinori opened the sleek Italian aperitivo bar in Hong Kong in 2023, and expanded the concept to Shanghai in 2025.

The article New NYC Bar Under Fire for Copying Name and Branding of World’s Best Bar appeared first on VinePair.
content:
As the global cohort of bartenders and industry enthusiasts gears up for this year’s announcement of the World’s 50 Best Bars tomorrow, last year’s victor Bar Leone in Hong Kong is soaking in its time at the top spot. And as it awaits this year’s ranking, the team at Bar Leone faces a less-expected obstacle: a new bar with the same name and near-identical branding that opened last month in New York City.

Rome native Lorenzo Antinori opened the sleek Italian aperitivo bar in Hong Kong in 2023, and expanded the concept to Shanghai in 2025. The Hong Kong outpost gained worldwide recognition when it was named No. 1 bar in the world last year by hospitality rankings site The 50, formerly known as 50 Best.

NYC’s Bar Leone — a two-storied bar doubling as a Martini lounge and Italian disco room — opened on Sept. 10 under the direction of Andres Diaz, who opened La Rubia and the now-closed Her Name Was Carmen.

When news of a stateside opening under the same name emerged in May, industry pros raised an eyebrow at the suspicious number of similarities. In response, the original Bar Leone issued a statement to make clear there was no association between the Hong Kong establishment and the NYC opening.

“We are not affiliated, associated, or in any way connected with the New York venue now trading under the Bar Leone name, and we have not authorized, licensed, endorsed, or sponsored it in any way,” reads the Important Announcement page on its website, which it added after learning of the NYC opening.

What remains unclear is whether or not NYC’s Bar Leone is an outright copycat.

The similarities are hard to ignore and go well beyond the name. The two share matching color palettes, comparable website designs, and near-identical logos of a sideways-facing lion holding a tray of Martinis.

Some industry insiders took to social media to critique Diaz’s bar for directly reprinting the name and aesthetic of the Hong Kong Bar. Bartenders of the 50 Best ilk are also suspicious of the NYC bar’s copycat name and branding.

“If they just called it Bar Leone, then okay, that would’ve been reasonable, but they’re completely ripping off someone else’s creativity, their branding, everything,” says NYC-based bartender Jonathan Adler, previously of Shinji’s and co-founder of soon-to-open Chiqui.

A spokesperson for the Bar Leone in NYC declined to comment other than stating “there is no correlation between the two venues.” VinePair also reached out to Bar Leone in Hong Kong, and the team reiterated the statement in its Important Announcement page.

The two bars differ the most in their respective concepts. The world-renowned Bar Leone offers a menu centered around classic Italian aperitivo drinks. Its motto is “Cocktail popolari,” which translates to “Cocktails for the people.” In NYC, Bar Leone is accessible “by invitation and reservation only” and brands itself as a “Martini lounge” that also serves “caviar, Champagne, and bites.”

“It’s like literally the polar opposite of what Bar Leone is all about, which is somewhere that everyone can go,” Adler says. “At this new place, the drinks range anywhere from $30 to $45. It’s the opposite of what people are asking for in New York right now.”

The new Bar Leone’s opening comes as bars that near the top of The 50’s annual list make the pitch to NYC. In 2025, Moe Aljaff and Juliette Larrouy opened the acclaimed cocktail bar schmuck. in NYC after working at the 50 Best-recognized Two Schmucks in Barcelona. Hong Kong’s Bar Leone admitted it is actively scoping out international expansion, including to the U.S., in its “Important Announcement” page — a venture with which the new Bar Leone could interfere.

Though there has been no direct indication of legal action between the two bars, Hong Kong-based Bar Leone’s announcement refers to the situation as an “active matter.”

They say imitation is the greatest form of flattery, but it seems NYC’s Bar Leone has sparked more anger than it has excitement.

“I’ve never seen anything this blatant,” Adler says. “They’re blatantly ripping it off.”

title: Beverage Programs Are Under Pressure. These Pros Are Finding Ways to Adapt.
summary:
It’s a hard time to run a beverage program. Costs are escalating due in part to an unhappy blend of tariffs, supply chain issues, and general inflation. The wholesale sector of the drinks industry is in a tremendous amount of flux following the collapse of Republic National Distributing Company (RNDC) over the last year, meaning that keeping steady supply of product is trickier than ever.

The article Beverage Programs Are Under Pressure. These Pros Are Finding Ways to Adapt. appeared first on VinePair.
content:
It’s a hard time to run a beverage program. Costs are escalating due in part to an unhappy blend of tariffs, supply chain issues, and general inflation. The wholesale sector of the drinks industry is in a tremendous amount of flux following the collapse of Republic National Distributing Company (RNDC) over the last year, meaning that keeping steady supply of product is trickier than ever. Add to that concerns over labor costs, a public that keeps hearing that no one drinks any more, and oh yeah, a bewildering array of products and product categories that could easily overwhelm even the most seasoned professional.

Yet savvy and experienced buyers and beverage directors are continuing to find ways to navigate the push and pull of excellent hospitality and the realities of business. Strategies abound for dealing with these challenges: some rely on economies of scale, or the ability to store large quantities of product, while others are contingent on knowing your clientele and how to deliver the experience they crave, even when the bottle they want most is either unavailable or has skyrocketed in price.

When Prices Soar

It’s absolutely not news to anyone that the cost of basically everything in beverage alcohol has increased, often dramatically, over the last half-decade or so. “I cannot sell Premier Cru Burgundy for the same price we could five years ago,” laments Will Jones, wine director at The Hope Farm and Little Bird in Fairhope, Ala. “So for something approachable, I may sell a Hautes-Côtes de Beaune or Hautes-Côtes de Nuits, or this really beautiful Bourgogne Rouge or Bourgogne Blanc.”

For the guest who maybe dreamed of a wine from an iconic region but is now suffering from sticker shock, “I can give someone a northern Italian or an Austrian or a German wine with as much of a story as I would for a Grand Cru Burgundy,” explains Felipe de Assis Villela, beverage director at Bluepoint Hospitality Group in Easton, Md. “I could give you a Grand Cru German wine for under $200, or you can get a Grand Cru Burgundy for $1,800, which, I’m not gonna stop you from doing, but that’s not what everyone’s able to do.”

While those substitutes can still excite guests, no one is thrilled about paying more and more money for their drinks. That’s compounded by pushing margins or markups ever higher, either because their clientele can and will pay the higher price or in a desperate attempt to wring a bit more profit out of what may be the main profit center of the property. Yet when the price of a bottle of wine, say, has potentially already been bumped up by the producer, the importer, and the distributor, an aggressive restaurant markup of 200-300 percent can be absolutely punishing to guests. “I’m not so obsessed with a percentage mark. That’s a luxury I have in my position,” admits de Assis Villela. A mix of common sense and a desire to actually move certain wines to help him set prices as opposed to pushing prices as high as possible has resulted in a program that maybe doesn’t boast a gaudy profit margin but does serve both guest and restaurant. “I’m still making money, but the percentage may not look like what I had to do on Long Island, which, you know, apologies to all my guests back there,” he says.

Buying in Bulk

One of the more straightforward ways to be more profitable is to purchase in larger quantities. While different states and different distributors can have wildly different approaches to volume discounts, most of the time if you’re willing to buy a bunch of cases of whatever, you’ll get a much better price. It can also insulate against product shortages, but of course it also requires something that not every restaurant or bar can have: storage space. Being able to place product at multiple different outlets within the same property or even the same city can also make bulk buying more viable.

“Sometimes distributors will set up quantity discounts for us,” notes Amanda Reed, director of beverage at E3 Co. Restaurant Group in Seattle. “We’ve gotta buy five cases at a time or 10 cases at a time — that’s usually our limit for storage in [most of our] properties. But if we’re coming up on a really good deal and there is plenty of supply, I might just try to work something out where we commit to X amount, but we’re only gonna bring it in five cases at a time.”

Accepting the Limits

Part of the challenge is the tremendous upheaval in the wholesale category over the last couple of years. The complete collapse of RNDC from the second-largest beverage wholesaler to Chapter 11 bankruptcy in less than two years has played no small part, with tariffs contributing not just to higher costs but also more challenges getting products into the U.S. in the first place.

Time, too, is at a premium, especially in a landscape where beverage professionals are often expected to perform any number of additional administrative and managerial tasks, even when that’s not exactly what attracted them to the job in the first place.

“When you first become a buyer, you’re so excited to sit down with reps and get to be this figure of authority,” says Johannus Grevelink, beverage director for José Andrés Group. “The reality is that if you open up my inbox every day, I have 40 to 60 emails from people about their product and how it could be a great fit at José Andrés Group or at one of our outlets with the name spelled wrong. Sifting through all that — I don’t know anyone that could have the time to do that.”

Hidden Costs

It’s relatively easy to understand much of what drives up prices at restaurants and bars, but there are plenty of less-obvious costs as well. Maintaining consistent placements doesn’t just make life easier for the beverage director or allow for lower prices on the product itself, it cuts down on training and printing costs, too.

In an era of ever-increasing labor costs, gathering staff to taste and train on new products is expensive. But that investment — in time, money, and effort — can also help new products thrive, especially in light of the alternative. “If I place a new spirit, I can send an email to a GM who will forward it to the AGM, who can print the tech sheet for pre-shift and talk to the staff about it,” says Grevelink. “Realistically, now that information has come through the supplier to the buyer to the GM to the AGM to maybe like a floor manager who’s doing pre-shift on a Tuesday. My passion for that bottle is not gonna translate.” Regular staff education and training can help move product, of course, but paying that hourly wage across the entire service team has never been so pricey.

Menu changes can also come with significant costs. “We don’t print our menus in house, we outsource,” says Reed. “So I have to be really selective about what I choose to put in the cocktails; I confirm that the inventory and availability is gonna be there. Once I’ve designed my cocktails, there’s a lot of back and forth between me and my reps about supply, because I don’t want to have to change one ingredient in the middle of a season when nothing else on the menu needs to be changed.”

This, again, is where larger buys (where possible) can come in handy. A program that changes less frequently can get by with less staff education, fewer menu changes, and require less admin time from frequently-overworked beverage directors and other managers. Yet every such person interviewed for this piece bemoaned that they were not able to spend as much time on some of those aspects of the job — staff training and increasing their own product knowledge most of all.

Managing Relationships

Just as the relationship with the guest is crucial to a great restaurant experience, everyone I spoke to was emphatic that their relationships with producers and suppliers was key to their work, both in terms of quality and in terms of job satisfaction. Cultivating and nourishing them is an active and intentional choice. “When we first opened at the Hope Farm, I was unable to get the large majority of any allocations that I wanted because we didn’t have that history,” says Jones. “Now thankfully, we do. I love meeting new winemakers. I love maintaining our connections with the ones that we love.” For Jones, it’s about far more than just getting access to product or even having something new and exciting to offer to guests. “I’m here to create a relationship with the producer, to host them in town and open a beautiful bottle of wine when they’re here, and to continue to build that relationship.”

That kind of relationship also just makes the day-to-day operation of a restaurant smoother. “I’m trying to avoid constantly running out of stuff and having to find a new vendor to fill a placement,” says James Baugh, beverage director for TMC Hospitality. “We want to build a long-term partnership with someone who supports us and has available product for us. And sometimes there’s just days where you blow through some product and it’s nice to have someone you know to ask, ‘hey, can you drop me a couple of things?’”

The overwhelming sense from beverage directors right now is that their job involves a consistent fight to keep their heads above water, to make sure that their programs can still meet guest needs while being leaner, more cost-conscious, and more resistant to staff and product turnover than ever before. They’re still passionate and motivated, but they’re also feeling the pressure and struggling to deal with it.

title: We Asked 11 Sommeliers: What’s the Most Underrated Napa Wine? (2026)
summary:
Napa has been one of the most esteemed winemaking regions in the world for decades. Known to churn out big, teeth-kicking Cabernet Sauvignons and bold Chardonnays, Napa is now synonymous with luxury wine among some drinkers. That said, the region offers a rich diversity beyond the most popular wineries and elite bottles. With vineyards stretching from the sun-drenched valley to high-altitude plots, Napa plays host to a wide diversity of grapes and vinification styles. And despite Napa’s mass acclaim, there are still some wines in the area that fly under the radar.

The article We Asked 11 Sommeliers: What’s the Most Underrated Napa Wine? (2026) appeared first on VinePair.
content:
Napa has been one of the most esteemed winemaking regions in the world for decades. Known to churn out big, teeth-kicking Cabernet Sauvignons and bold Chardonnays, Napa is now synonymous with luxury wine among some drinkers. That said, the region offers a rich diversity beyond the most popular wineries and elite bottles.

With vineyards stretching from the sun-drenched valley to high-altitude plots, Napa plays host to a wide diversity of grapes and vinification styles. And despite Napa’s mass acclaim, there are still some wines in the area that fly under the radar. That’s why we tapped sommeliers from across the country to name the Napa wines that they think are ripe for more attention.

Ranging from old-school Cabernets to sparkling wines, these are the Napa wines that sommeliers think deserve some more love.

The most underrated Napa wines, according to sommeliers:

  • Pilcrow Granite Lake Cabernet Sauvignon
  • Scholium Project Pergamos Cabernet Sauvignon 2024
  • Chardonnay
  • Stony Hill Chardonnay
  • Domaine Carneros Brut Vintage Cuvée
  • Mayacamas Vineyards Chardonnay 2020
  • Cabernet Franc
  • Enfield Wine Co.
  • Cain Vineyards & Winery Cain Five
  • Component Wine Co. Petit Verdot
  • Matthiasson Wines
  • Locanda Beckstoffer Georges III Cabernet Sauvignon

“Pilcrow’s Granite Lake Cabernet Sauvignon. It has all the intensity and structure of great mountain Cabernet, but Pilcrow turns the volume down — lower alcohol, restrained oak, bright acidity, and a distinctly savory, mineral character. It feels more like a glimpse into old-school Napa than another modern cult Cabernet. For me, Granite Lake is Pilcrow’s best wine, and it deserves to be mentioned alongside far more famous Napa Cabernets.” —Andrew Albert, sommelier, Cru Uncorked, Moreland Hills, Ohio

“My underrated Napa wine is Abe Schoener’s Mt. Veeder Cabernet Sauvignon from his ‘Scholium Project’ label. The vines at a higher altitude give a cooler, mountainous tone that balances the fruit’s deep body. I love Abe’s experimental style — this wine combines intrigue and unexpected freshness with a really satisfying texture you’d crave from a Napa Cab.” —Bethany Heinze, co-owner and beverage director, Vern’s, Charleston, S.C.

“I firmly believe Chardonnay is one of Napa Valley’s most underrated wines. The western side of the valley is home to incredible producers like Stony Hill, Staglin, and Heitz Cellars, crafting wines that are stunning upon release but truly shine with age. I’ve had the pleasure of tasting older vintages of Stony Hill that have absolutely blown me away. The best part is that you can find beautifully aged Napa Chardonnay for a fraction of what you’d pay for comparable white Burgundy.” —Juan Valencia, sommelier, Ômo by Jônt, Winter Park, Colo.

“Domaine Carneros sparkling wine. With a climate and variety of quality soils ideal for Chardonnay and Pinot Noir, the Los Carneros AVA in the Napa Valley produces outstanding — though often underrated — méthode traditionnelle sparkling wine. Domaine Carneros (by Taittinger) stands out for its use of 100 percent Los Carneros AVA grapes that are sustainably farmed, meticulously blended, and aged at least three years on the lees. The result is a light, crisp, and structured wine with significant minerality. Within its broad sparkling portfolio, the lovely Vintage Estate Brut Cuvée is a great value and readily available. It’s featured in my Bahamian wine cellar.” —Harlan Spiva, sommelier, Grand Hyatt Baha Mar, Nassau, Bahamas

“Mayacamas Vineyards Chardonnay 2020. This was an extremely difficult vintage, but Mayacamas Vineyards over-delivered through its high elevation and Old World winemaking style. This is a luxury bracket wine priced at only $50 to $60 per bottle. For those wanting an old-school, pre-ABC (Anything But Chardonnay) Napa experience inspired by the great white Burgundies of Meursault and the flinty minerality of Pouilly-Fuissé, look no further.” —Ryan Furlan, lead sommelier, La Grande Boucherie, Chicago

“One of the most underrated wines coming out of Napa Valley today is Cabernet Franc. Napa is naturally associated with Cabernet Sauvignon, but Cabernet Franc offers incredible aromatic complexity, freshness, and elegance while still reflecting the valley’s world-class terroir. Its notes of violet, graphite, red fruit, and spice make it exceptionally versatile at the dining table and a great option for guests looking to explore Napa beyond its most famous variety. At my restaurants, guests often default to Cabernet Sauvignon, but Cabernet Franc provides the same sense of place with more brightness, aromatic lift, and food versatility.” —Adil Berrady, director of food and beverage, Kimpton Gray Hotel, Vol. 39, and Boleo, Chicago

“Enfield Wine Co. Not everything John Lockwood makes is technically Napa, as some of the vineyards he sources from sit just over the border, but the winery as a whole represents a style of Napa that people don’t always think about. All of his wines show restraint and a sense of place. They’re interesting and delicious without trying too hard, and they’re a great reminder that there’s a lot more happening in and around Napa than big Cab and rich Chard.” —Andrew Limberg, director of operations and Sommelier, Moon Rabbit, Washington, D.C.

“My favorite underrated producer in Napa has got to be Cain Vineyards & Winery. Located on Spring Mountain, it lost nearly all of its vineyard land during the Glass Fire in 2020 but has since replanted. The knowledge and the hospitality they provide is amazing. The winery’s flagship bottle, Cain Five, is a showstopper at any age and provides incredible value — especially when released as a library wine.” —Gabriel Corbett, sommelier, Hive Hospitality, Washington, D.C.

“If you’re looking for the most underrated wine in Napa, I’d point you to Component Wine Co.’s Petit Verdot. Marc Gagnon is definitely not one to shy away from a challenge — Petit Verdot has one of the longest ripening cycles of any grape, and he pulls it off beautifully every single year. Only 600 bottles are made annually, so it’s not easy to find, but trust me — when you do see it, grab it.” —Andrey Ivanov, master sommelier, Nisei; owner, Bliss Wine Concierge, San Francisco

“Matthiasson is one of the producers I consistently come back to when talking about the breadth of what Napa can be. Steve and Jill Matthiasson have built a program equally around farming and wine making, letting individual varieties and sites speak for themselves. Of course, they make Cabernet, but some of the most compelling wines are things like Ribolla Gialla, Refosco, and their white blend. For a region that is so often defined by one or two particular styles of wine, Matthiasson is a great reminder of just how diverse Napa can be.” —Sean Lowder, director of operations, Liberty Restaurant Group, Arlington, Va.

“My choice would be Locanda. I think the Beckstoffer Georges III Cabernet expression is comparable to other iconic wines selling for three times the price at restaurants. It’s truly stellar and, for the quality and pedigree, feels like an especially compelling bottle. The wine has the depth and complexity you’d expect from a much more expensive pour, while still feeling like a thoughtful value on the list.” —Gene Dexter, wine specialist, Lotte and Charlotte, Seattle

title: Why Did a Hot Take on Bartender Guest Shifts Spark a Social Media Firestorm?
summary:
Hot takes are like a bowl of shishito peppers. They’re mild most of the time, but the potential for one to be packed with an intense spice always lurks. In August, the bar community learned that a hot take beginning with the phrase “No one cares about your f*cking guest shift” contained enough Scoville units to cause an uncomfortable burning sensation. The source of the pain came from the appropriately-titled Hospitality Hot Takes, a typically lighthearted Instagram series where Los Angeles-based bartender and content creator Saeed “Hawk” House asks bartenders their snappy opinions on the state of the industry.

The article Why Did a Hot Take on Bartender Guest Shifts Spark a Social Media Firestorm? appeared first on VinePair.
content:
Hot takes are like a bowl of shishito peppers. They’re mild most of the time, but the potential for one to be packed with an intense spice always lurks. In August, the bar community learned that a hot take beginning with the phrase “No one cares about your f*cking guest shift” contained enough Scoville units to cause an uncomfortable burning sensation.

The source of the pain came from the appropriately-titled Hospitality Hot Takes, a typically lighthearted Instagram series where Los Angeles-based bartender and content creator Saeed “Hawk” House asks bartenders their snappy opinions on the state of the industry. On August 17, House dropped a video featuring Kate Gerwin, in which the influential owner of Happy Accidents in Albuquerque and soon-to-be-open Bad Apple in Houston went scorched earth on guest shifts.

Each barb within the video’s near-three-minute run time was pointed and piquant: They exist for bars to chase awards and for bartenders to hang out with friends. Brands waste money on them instead of putting funds toward job retention. They alienate regular customers. At one point during the interview, Gerwin said “I wanna see ‘em go away.”

Reactions to the video were swift and abundant. Plenty of people championed Gerwin’s opinion. Others pushed back, with some accusing her of hypocrisy based on her long record of participating in guest shifts around the world. The impetus behind most of her talking points isn’t necessarily new or out of left field, but her remarks caused what looks like, in retrospect, a simmering pot to boil over. But how much of a mess is there to clean up in its wake?

Why Now?

House usually isn’t one to speculate on which of his hot take videos may generate buzz. His chat with Gerwin was slightly different. “The moment I filmed it, I knew it was going to be a little hot,” he says. “But I wasn’t prepared for what was to come after it was posted.”

He wasn’t wrong. The post has generated 285,000 views, 12,200 likes, and 782 comments as of this writing. It’s the highest number in each category of any post within the series: his hot takes average around 13,000 views per day, and the most popular posts usually pick up 1,000 – to 2,000 likes and 100 to 200 comments. Part of his gut instinct stemmed from knowing who he was interviewing. “If it was someone else, I don’t think it would have done much,” he explains. “But because it was Kate, and because she’s done so many guest shifts, it generated much more heat.”

Gerwin also didn’t expect her take to go viral, even if she also knew it was spicy. She suspects part of the reason why it did also has something to do with who she is and not necessarily what she said — but not in the way House speculates.

“If it was a man that said it, the hot take wouldn’t have tracked,” she says. “Last year, a well-known male industry figure made a public comment about World’s 50 Best, saying ‘welcome to the circle jerk,’ and nobody said a single word.”

Regardless of the reason why, the hot take went viral and generated its fair share of even hotter comments. While Gerwin admits to not fully watching the finished product, she’s also aware the snap reactionary nature of hot takes means the main point she wanted to get across was likely lost in the fervor. As the heat cools over time, she hopes the root of her point becomes clearer. She doesn’t inherently hate the idea of guest shifts. She despises the purpose behind some of the industry’s more prominent guest shift events.

A Gateway to a Bigger Issue

Gerwin’s not shy about discussing how guest shifts fueled her global travels over the years. She also knows this makes her an easy target for claims of hypocrisy. But she also says these very travels make her well-qualified to call out the elements that make guest shifts problematic.

“People say ‘why should you be the one talking about it?’ Well, I’m the authority on the subject because I do more guest shifts than anyone. I’m the person that should be talking about this,” she says. “And I know that I’m calling out my own benefit. I have way more to lose, and I am putting some of my own perks at risk, such as getting flown to places around the world.”

Gerwin’s guest shift globetrotting has indeed provided her a glimpse behind the curtain. She says she’s gathered enough experiential intel along the way to develop disdain for how some bars use guest shifts as nothing more than leverage to gain favor with awards organizations. The lion’s share of her ire is toward 50 Best, the awards group that recently rebranded as The 50. She views the group as a ‘pay-for-play’-driven collective that’s created an unsavory ecosystem among bars who desire the attention generated by a bright red 50 Best scarf.

“There are bars that are ‘50 Best chasers,’ and we know who the chasers are,” she says. “There are some bars I’ve done guest shifts in, and those shifts have never happened without a 50 Best voter in attendance.”

“I wasn’t prepared for what was to come after it was posted.”

These ‘chasers,’ according to Gerwin, hold guest shifts strictly to gain favor with the journalists, bartenders, and cocktail aficionados who make up 50 Best’s judging collective. In order to fund these guest shifts that gain exposure to voters, bars get brand sponsorship. To Gerwin, this creates a systemic pattern she finds ultimately damaging to the bar community writ large. “Brands are spending money on these guest shifts, while they’re also laying off brand ambassadors and other brand employees,” she says. “That’s a problem.”

Gerwin also states this type of accolades-driven guest shift, coupled with 50 Best’s lack of official criteria behind the voting process, can lay the groundwork for shady activities.

“There are also vote swaps that happen — ‘vote for my bar and we’ll get you a vote for 50 Best’,” she says. “I’ve been approached by people that have never been to my bar to ask if I wanted to vote for their bar in exchange for a vote swap. I told them no. It’s corrupt and mind-numbingly disgusting.”

Gerwin notes this pattern of guest shift behavior is a far bigger issue in Europe and Asia than it is in the U.S., primarily because a 50 Best listing isn’t comparable to the domestic clout that a Tales of the Cocktail nomination can deliver. Still, it’s a big enough issue to compel her to potentially bite the hand that feeds her global guest shift opportunities, partially because she feels that people like her speaking out on the subject is the only way to bring the broken parts of guest shift culture to light.

“50 Best’s parent company William Reed generated more than £80 million in revenue last year, so they don’t care about changing the judging process even if it’s corrupt,” she says. “To them, 50 Best is a money-making machine. Guest shifts are part of that machine.”

Of course, extrapolating this fuller context from a rapid-fire hot take is simply not possible. Gerwin understands this, and part of this understanding involves her reiterating that she’s not on some crusade to stop all guest shifts. Despite her “I wanna see ‘em go away” chirp in the video, she’s a strong supporter of guest shifts held for fundraising or events designed to build and uplift communities. Her primary intention behind her comments is to spark a conversation within the industry about how to best jettison the baggage that can weigh down guest shift culture.

A Chance for Deeper Reflection

Pushing aside Gerwin’s chief issue still leaves crumbs of guest shift criticism to discuss: They’re held so industry friends can hang out together. They’re designed to placate the ego of the visiting bartender with enough clout to be an industry known commodity. The money brands use to sponsor the events may be better spent on their own human capital during crummy economic times. These talking points sparked deeper reflection among the people who participated in the comments, not to mention the host.

“Kate’s comments made me think about why I do my guest shifts — am I doing it just for the ego, or is it because I am legitimately excited to dust off some of my bartending skills, serve people, and be creative?” says House. “Also, is my brand-sponsored shift coming at the cost of someone else’s job?”

“Guest shifts have absolutely been used to climb a popularity ladder, where I believe some folks may feel this is disingenuous or like guest shifts are an unapproachable ‘cool kids club,’ explains Kapri Robinson, bar consultant, bartender at Allegory in Washington D.C., president of the BIPOC advocacy group Chocolate City’s Best, and comment thread participant. “I think breaking down those walls for guest shifts is important. Just the feeling that there’s an inner circle that makes guest shifts feel unattainable or unwelcoming should be dismantled altogether.”

“With guest shifts, everyone is running around in the same, small circle. If you’re in a small circle like that, you just go back and forth. You don’t really give yourself a chance to break out of that circle and go to smaller places to see what they do.”

At the same time, there’s enough room to consider some of the positive elements that can come from a guest shift when they’re done with a more noble cause in mind. “Guest shifts can be a nuanced thing, which can make it a good thing,” explains Mike Guzmán, creative director of Blue Door in Charlotte, N.C and, like Robinson, a voice in the comment thread. “Bringing guest bartenders to our backyard is important to expand our community. Plus, it can give our local guests an opportunity to have drinks they may otherwise never get a chance to drink.”

For Guzmán, hosting an occasional guest shift at his bar can be crucial in a city like Charlotte, a secondary market that’s still trying to figure out how to build a robust cocktail bar scene. He sees them as an opportunity to satiate the community’s increasingly ravenous hunger for knowledge, which is why he requests all guest shift participants to host an education-focused seminar in the afternoon before they get behind the stick. The difficult part for him, and other bartenders in similar markets, is getting bars from larger markets to commit.

“With guest shifts, everyone is running around in the same, small circle,” he says. “If you’re in a small circle like that, you just go back and forth. You don’t really give yourself a chance to break out of that circle and go to smaller places to see what they do. That’s why it was so great to see Cobra from Columbus, Ohio win their Tales’ award for Best U.S. Restaurant Bar. We need more of that.”

Even if that circle is small, the footprint left by those engaging in guest shifts within the circle is quite large. These special shifts afford bartenders opportunities to not only travel the world, but to bring the world to their home. While guest shifts involving long-haul plane rides and international border crossings can produce jaded feelings because of the awards circuit, they can nonetheless provide something positive for those that wish to connect and grow professionally and beyond.

“Personally, guest shifts were the reason I got to see the world,” Robinson says. “Guest shifts were not something I thought was possible for me in this industry, but they are something that opened doors not only for me but also for my team to travel and learn.

“Not only that, but we were able to host a few awesome bars and bartenders at Allegory that then became long-standing relationships in our futures,” she continues. “That exchange, and being able to show off Washington D.C. as part of the exchange, I believe is worth one night of having another bar behind our bar.”

A Study in Duality

In the Hospitality Hot Takes comments section, the phrase “two things can be true” made multiple appearances. Gerwin even said it during her interview. If her hot take does indeed spark a long-lasting conversation of guest shifts, this dichotomy seems like a fitting mantra to anchor such chatter. A guest shift held solely for award-chasing ambition may rankle individuals, but they’re as likely to continue as the guest shifts put on for community-driven reasons. Speaking for or against guest shift culture will likely need some sort of qualification.

This oddly enough brings us back to the shishito pepper. The guest shifts held to cajole votes may be akin to that one spicy outlier in a bowl, which may leave an unpleasant taste behind. The rest of the bowl, however, may be comparable to the guest shifts which aim to build community and promote genuine camaraderie within the industry. These shifts, when executed properly, can be quite good — and perhaps good enough to keep them on the bar world’s menu for the foreseeable future.

title: A Visual Guide to Europe’s Most Popular Olive Oil Varieties, From Koroneiki to Picual [MAP]
summary:
Throughout Europe, there’s a rich diversity of olive varieties. The continent’s warmer, Mediterranean regions are especially abundant in the crop, with a number of notable varieties coming from Spain, Italy, Greece, France, and Portugal. But while some cultivars might be best suited for snacking or for mixing up a batch of Dirty Martinis, others are best known for their role in olive oil production. Due to the wide variety of olive types, the corresponding olive oils range in flavor from buttery and silky to piquant and spicy.

content:
Throughout Europe, there’s a rich diversity of olive varieties. The continent’s warmer, Mediterranean regions are especially abundant in the crop, with a number of notable varieties coming from Spain, Italy, Greece, France, and Portugal. But while some cultivars might be best suited for snacking or for mixing up a batch of Dirty Martinis, others are best known for their role in olive oil production.

Due to the wide variety of olive types, the corresponding olive oils range in flavor from buttery and silky to piquant and spicy. And the inherent characteristics of each cultivar — such as size and natural fat content — inform its corresponding oil’s look and taste. One of the most significant factors in shaping the flavor of an olive oil is the fruit’s polyphenol content. Polyphenols are compounds that bring a peppery, back-of-the-throat spice, and such olive oils are often reserved for dressing dishes as a flavorful finishing touch. On the other hand, low-polyphenol olive oils deliver a silky mouthfeel and neutral flavors, and are usually used for cooking over heat.

Before grabbing any olive oil off the grocery store shelf, read on to discover which cultivars produce the oils best suited to your needs.

Portugal

Cobrançosa

Often thought of as the counterpart to Galega in Portuguese olive oil, Cobrançosa comes from northern regions like Trás-os-Montes. Its oil is all-things power: The nose is a bouquet of herbs, and the palate brings the bold, peppery, and bitter profile that will nag at the back of the tongue. Its intensity is a result of a high polyphenol content, and it is often blended with Galega to produce a well-balanced oil. Galega oil brings a rounded sweetness, and Cobrançosa oil delivers a punchy structure.

Galega

Galega is Portugal’s most planted olive cultivar, popular in the country’s southern regions like Ribatejo, Alentejo, and Algarve. In turn, the variety is one of the most common in Portuguese cooking. Galegas are small olives and, with a relatively low polyphenol content, offer a sweet and mild flavor to the oil. Galega oil has a delicate texture, bringing little to no peppery bite at the end. Where it shines in palatability, Galega oil lacks in verve — and to compensate, it is often blended with Cobrançosa.

Spain

Arbequina

Arbequina olives come from Spain’s Catalonia region but are now a popular olive cultivar grown across the globe. The variety’s trees are easily identifiable, as they are smaller and sparser than those of other cultivars. Arbequina oil is appreciated for its fruity and delicate character, with little to no spice or bitterness.

Hojiblanca

Hojiblanca olives are indigenous to Andalusia in the south of Spain. The variety is well adapted to the region’s intense heat and dryness, making it a reliable cultivar for olive oil production. Hojiblanca oil is bold, grassy, and slightly peppery, balanced by sweet notes of fruit and almonds. As a result, home cooks and chefs alike prize Hojiblanca oil for its versatility: Its high smoke point makes it suitable for cooking, and its strong flavor makes it ideal to be used as a dressing.

Picual

Picual is the most widely planted olive in Spain, and possibly in the world. Also hailing from Andalusia, Picual olives are relatively high in oil content, making them a favorable cultivar for olive oil producers. The corresponding oil tastes aromatic and fruity on the front with a bouquet of herbaceous and tropical flavors on the back. The olive’s high polyphenol content also delivers a bright, zippy edge to the oil.

France

Aglandau

Grown in and around the Provence region in southern France, Aglandau olives are some of the most common in Mediterranean dishes. But their high oil content, coming in at around 20 percent, also makes the cultivar a viable choice for olive oil. Its extra virgin extract is most common in Mediterranean cuisine for dressings and dips, though it is sometimes used for cooking over heat as well. Aglandau oil brings a fruit-forward palate, with background flavors of artichoke and almond. Aglandaus are typically harvested just before they’re ripe, resulting in a lively and bright oil with a tinge of pepper at the back.

Tanche

Also coming from Provence are Tanche olives, dark purple to black in color with a mild, mature flavor. Tanches are the same variety as the renowned Nyons olive — named after the specific area where they grow — and were the first cultivar to join France’s AOP system. Producers tend to harvest the cultivar after the fruit is fully ripe to result in sweet, jammy flavor and a full-bodied, unctuous mouthfeel. Expect a velvety texture to bring about notes of green apple, dried fruit, and toasted nuts.

Cailletier

Better known as the fan-favorite, small and dark Niçoise olive, the Cailletier cultivar grows around the Alpes-Maritimes region in the southeast of France. It is the variety used to produce the famous huile de Nice (oil from Nice), prized for its blend of smooth, fruity flavors with a bouncy bitterness. Cailletier oil is almost ubiquitous in Niçoise cuisine — a style of cooking that brings together ingredients from both southern France and northern Italy.

Italy

Castelvetrano

Castelvetrano olives may be better known for snacking or dirtying Martinis, but it’s also common for the Sicilian cultivar to be pressed for its oil. When consumed whole or as the oil, these olives bring a silky mouthfeel and buttery taste. For olive oil production, this variety is better known as Nocellara del Belice, a classification protected under Italy’s Protected Designation of Origin (DOP) system.

Coratina

Coming from Puglia, Coratina is notorious for being one of the spiciest, most bitter olive oils out there. Around the region, massive Coratina trees grow in groves that extend for miles. On the palate, Coratina oil begins with a burst of fruit that leads into a grassy, peppery kick on the finish. That sharp, spicy bite is a result of its high polyphenol content. The cultivar’s oil is mainly used for finishing dishes or for dipping, but make sure to not use too much, lest the spice become overwhelming.

Frantoio

Frantoio olives come from the hot, rolling hills of Tuscany. When mature, Frantoios range anywhere from dark purple to black, but they are usually harvested just as the color changes from green to preserve their vibrance in flavor. These olives are high in oil content — around 25 percent of the fruit is oil — and produce sweet, earthy flavors of grass, artichoke, and green apple. The finish is bitter and peppery, a complexity that makes this cultivar’s oils a go-to for finishing dishes rather than cooking.

Leccino

Leccino olives originated in Tuscany but are now cultivated in the neighboring region of Umbria as well. The cultivar — grown on large, drooping trees — is used to produce both olive oil and black table olives. Leccinos are high in fat content, and depending on the harvest time, the oil can range from fruity and intense to neutral and almost flavorless. That versatility makes Leccino oil common for both cooking and dressing.

Taggiasca

Coming from Liguria, Taggiasca olives look like a kaleidoscope on a tree: On the same plant, the olives’ colors can range from green to brown to purple. Taggiascas boast a relatively low water content, lending a lively and powerful flavor. The resulting oil is bright and fruity with nuances of sweet almonds. However, the olive’s low polyphenol content doesn’t impart much of a bite. Instead, Taggiasca oil is known to be silky and buttery.

Greece

Koroneiki

Koroneiki olives come from Peloponnese, a large region in southern Greece. The Koroneiki trees yield high volumes of small, polyphenol-rich olives. As a result, the olives are prized for their oils that deliver vibrant flavors of pepper, grass, and herbs. The prestigious oil is most often used for dressing dishes, but some chefs like to use it in low- to medium-heat cooking scenarios to impart that strong, bright flavor.

*Image retrieved from Skyler Ewing via unsplash.com

title: Where To Drink in NYC Right Now (October 2026)
summary:
When the VinePair team isn’t busy working at HQ, we’re in the field doing what we do best: scoping out the best cocktails, wine, and beer in the five boroughs. Here are the cool, current, and flat-out excellent bars and restaurants you should visit in New York right now, according to our editors. Check here each month for an updated list of where to drink in New York City. New to the list this month: Amphora, Bar CC, Graciela, Bar Etienne, and Don’t By Shy.

The article Where To Drink in NYC Right Now (October 2026) appeared first on VinePair.
content:
When the VinePair team isn’t busy working at HQ, we’re in the field doing what we do best: scoping out the best cocktails, wine, and beer in the five boroughs. Here are the cool, current, and flat-out excellent bars and restaurants you should visit in New York right now, according to our editors.

Check here each month for an updated list of where to drink in New York City. New to the list this month: Amphora, Bar CC, Graciela, Bar Etienne, and Don’t By Shy.

Bar Chimera

550 Madison Ave, New York, NY 10022

Part of Gracious Hospitality’s massive Midtown expansion — including a new location of Cote and a forthcoming omakase restaurant — Bar Chimera brings together three distinct drinking concepts: Martinis, whiskey, and wine. The luxurious space focuses on splurge-worthy drinks including an extensive program of aged Madeiras, special pours of hard-to-find wines and spirits, and classic Martinis made with meticulously thought-out ingredients, even down to the water used to dilute the drink.

Website

Amphora

43 E 20th St, New York, NY 10003

The iconic space that once housed wine-focused restaurants Veritas and Saint Urban is back as Amphora, and like its predecessors, it has a heavy-hitting wine list. The seasonal tasting menu from executive chef Jack Logue can be accompanied by pairings curated by wine director Chris Miller, or guests can dig into the vast cellar of over 2,500 labels.

Website

Bar CC

85 10th Ave, New York, NY 10011

The team behind Chelsea’s swanky Crane Club is expanding with an equally luxe cocktail bar — complete with floor-to-ceiling drapery, velvet fabric walls, and hand-blown Venetian sconces. For this project, chef Melissa Rodriguez and restaurateur Jeff Katz tapped acclaimed bartender Harrison Ginsberg (previously of Overstory) to design the cocktail program. Bar CC’s menu features elegant takes on classics like the CC Martini made with a savory olive, pepper, and mignonette brine, and the Toasted Almond Sour, with gin, toasted almond, lemon, and Italian meringue.

Website

Graciela

81 Greenwich Ave, New York, NY 10014

Graciela is an Argentine tavern and steakhouse from Pablo Rivero, the restaurateur behind Buenos Aires destination Don Julio. Though the showy live-fire cooking and big cuts of meat are center stage, the menu offers an impressive range of must-order starters like the cheesy brócoli dip with almonds and breadcrumbs and the perfectly dense chickpea tart with provolone and smoked paprika. The lengthy wine list offers an appealing set of global selections, but it’s hard to ignore the call to go all-in on the Argentina of it all. The program goes far beyond the obligatory Malbec, showcasing interesting bottles and producers not often seen on NYC lists. We recommend chatting with the wonderful team led by beverage director Jirka Jireh Rivera, to learn more about these lesser-known bottles the country has to offer, from high-elevation Sémillon to old-vine Bastardo.

Website

Bar Etienne

44 Bedford St, New York, NY 10014

Another addition to downtown’s growing list of scene-y bars to sip a spritz and a tomato-adorned Martini, Bar Etienne recently opened in the former Bandits space in the West Village. The casual neighborhood spot from longtime friends and hospitality veterans Michael Bray and Keith Larry features a French bistro-inspired menu and a playful list of culinary-minded cocktails like the Banana Question, made with rum and clarified banana, and the Petite Pompette with strawberry infused Pimm’s and mint. And be sure to check out the menu of teeny ’tinis, including classic, dirty, mushroom, and tomato variations.

Website

Somssi

79 MacDougal St, New York, NY 10012

Somssi is a new restaurant from the team at NA:EUN Hospitality — the group behind acclaimed concepts Atoboy, Atomix, and NARO — spearheaded by the group’s former director of operations Ahris Kim. Between the diverse menu of shareable plates and the extensive selection of wine, sake, and cocktails, there are countless pairing permutations to be made here. One that calls to us is the Potato, Potato, Potato, and caviar, which neatly wraps a creamy pomme purée with thin, crispy potato strings, topped with a heap of caviar, of course, which we’re sure would go well with a sparkling wine from the Finger Lakes or even a spritzy sake. The menu is a treasure trove of interesting beverages, so whichever combo you go with, it’s bound to be a delightful drinking experience.

Website

Dean’s

213 6th Ave, New York, NY 10014

Just when we thought NYC’s Guinness mania couldn’t go any longer, Dean’s arrives in the West Village ready to pour you a perfect — and sometimes even oyster-topped — pint. The British pub-inspired spot from Jess Shadbolt and Annie Shi of King stays true to its theme with dishes like fish and chips, stargazy pie, and pork scratchings plus a list of English sparkling to wash it all down.

Website

Don’t Be Shy

68 Charlton St, New York, NY 10014

The latest in a string of cocktail bars inspired by Japanese craftsmanship and hospitality, Don’t Be Shy is a sleek new spot in Hudson Square inspired by the bars of Tokyo’s polished Ginza neighborhood. The signature “Trip to Japan” cocktails showcase Japanese flavors like the Edo, made with sweet potato miso flavored vodka, and the refreshing Echigo, which combines sparkling sake with Echigo stout beer.

Website

Noury

137 Sullivan St, New York, NY 10012

From Lina Goujjane and Alex Chang, the wife-and-husband team behind Hudson Square’s Kiko, Noury combines elements of a modern Japanese izakaya with those of a wine and sake bar. Here, guests can pair small bites like the daily selection of sashimi or the house vegetable futomaki with rare bottles of sake or splurge-worthy Champagnes.

Website

Bar Monto

61 2nd Ave, New York, NY 10003

If you’ve been keeping up with New York’s boom in modern Irish pubs, here’s another one to add to your list. Bar Monto is the latest laid-back spot slinging creamy pints of Guinness in custom glassware. Beyond beer, the bar also offers a fun list of straightforward yet complex cocktails like the Basque Connection, made with Boatyard Irish gin, sherry, Valentia Island Irish vermouth, tonic, and muddled orange. The space draws inspiration from the pubs and social clubs found in Ireland in the 1980s and ’90s and aims to be a center for community, collaborating with local artists and musicians for events.

Website

Tin’s

109 Ludlow St, New York, NY 10002

Tin’s is a multi-concept space from Philip Dizard and Mercury Tin, bringing together their love for New York bars and Shanghainese comfort food in a three-story experience that includes both a casual dumpling counter and high-end cocktail bar. Creative concoctions span from unexpected delights like the Timmy’s Brain Blaster, a bright-green frozen Cognac cocktail topped with salted mascarpone foam, to riffs on classics like the Dako-Ri, a classic Daiquiri made with maojian tea and lemongrass.

Website

Oriana

174 Mott St, New York, NY 10012

Oriana is the wood-fired follow-up to West Village restaurant The Noortwyck, from executive chef Andy Quinn and acclaimed sommelier Cedric Nicaise. The new Nolita spot focuses on live-fire cooking, with a menu of dishes prepared over a wood-fired grill. To accompany plates like the BBQ Duck Crown and Axe Handle Pork Chop, Oriana features a deep, 7,000-bottle cellar, primarily composed of classic European wines. Though there are certainly many opportunities to splurge, the program also features over 150 bottles under $100.

Website

Bar Chucho

37 Market St, New York, NY 10002

Fans of Corima’s Uni Gin Sour, rejoice! The (somewhat controversial) savory cocktail is making its return at Bar Chucho, a new bar from the team behind the acclaimed Mexican tasting menu spot that first dared to shake sea urchin with booze. Though the walk-in-only space has a more casual, cantina-like vibe, the high-concept cocktails and bar snacks still show off complex flavors. The drink menu includes riffs on classics like the Margarita with Granny Smith apple, Midori, and cilantro and a mezcal-based Sazerac with plantain and hoja santa. And we can’t forget the Uni Gin Sour — now served on draft — revamped with strawberry and yuzu. Bar snacks include a cheesy mushroom gringa, tuna chilindrina, and a dry-aged burger with bone marrow and burnt onion mayo.

Website

Echo Lake

357 Grand St, Brooklyn, NY 11211

This new two-story bar concept in Williamsburg is entirely focused on celebrating rum. The first floor, Echo Lake, showcases the versatile spirit in a range of cocktails, from classic spirit-forward creations to fruit-filled tropical drinks. It also offers a full menu of Daiquiri variations, including a rotating “Daily Daiquiri” for just $12. Head downstairs to Undercurrent to dive deeper into the spirit with special pours from rare and hard to find bottles.

Website

Kinda Nice

168 Borinquen Pl, Brooklyn, NY 11211

Known for their work behind the bar at Brooklyn’s beloved Grand Army, Patty Dennison and Ally Marrone are going out on their own with their new venture Kinda Nice. The welcoming Williamsburg cocktail bar brings the convivial feeling of an old-school neighborhood diner, with the food and drinks to match. The cocktails are based on classic diner favorites, including a Greek Salad ‘Tini and a Short Stack Margarita (with a choice between strawberry and blueberry flavors).

Website

Titán

5 Front St, Brooklyn, NY 11201

With chef Alan Delgado of flour-tortilla destination Los Burritos Juarez designing the menu and esteemed bartender Ivy Mix, previously of beloved agave bar Leyenda and current co-owner of Whoopsie Daisy, shaking up drinks, Dumbo’s new Titán brings two buzzy names from New York’s food and drink scenes into one beautifully curated space. The drinks menu offers expertly executed classics like a Margarita and Michelada, as well as culinary-inspired cocktails like the Dirty Root, with bacanora and escabeche, and the frozen Charmagoy, which brings together tequila, tamarind, mango, and chamoy.

Website

Frenzie

129 Atlantic Ave, Brooklyn, NY 11201

 

The team behind Brooklyn’s Confidant is expanding with a casual pizza spot that caters to the late-night crowd. While Frenzie is sure to be a great place to enjoy a bottle of chilled red wine and a spicy vodka pie at any time, it’s worth noting that at 10 p.m. the restaurant offers a few combo deals that make for the perfect nightcap (every night out should end with a slice). The offer, available Thursday, Friday, and Saturday, pairs a cheese or pepperoni pie with either a pitcher of Narragansett beer, two Daiquiris, or two Martinis.

Website

Grimm Tavern

659 Vanderbilt Ave, Brooklyn, NY 11238

Lauren and Joe Gimm, the couple behind East Williamsburg’s beloved brewery Grimm Artisanal Ales, recently debuted their new restaurant Grimm Tavern. Here guests can explore Grimm’s extensive list of beers alongside classic American tavern dishes like a dry-aged smash burger and a muffuletta. But it isn’t just for beer fans; the menu also features a selection of wines from Grimm’s project Physica Wines as well as a list of signature cocktails.

Website

Zig Zag Oyster Bar

406 Prospect Pl, Brooklyn, NY 11238

The team behind Lower East Side seafood hot spot Cervo’s now has a dedicated raw bar in Brooklyn. If indulging in a seafood tower could ever be considered casual, this vibey, walk-in only spot might be the place. Grab a seat on the sidewalk or along the space’s stunning curved bar and order an Original Martini or Bloody Mary to accompany the icy plates of oysters and shrimp cocktail.

Website

Bar Ferdinando

151 Union St, Brooklyn, NY 11231

Bar Ferdinando is an Italian bar and café that recently took over the space of beloved Carroll Gardens institution Ferdinando’s Focacceria, which served the neighborhood for 121 years. The revamped space pairs Sicilian snacks with classic aperitivo drinks and a wide selection of amari. It’s the ideal location for an afternoon of sipping Negronis, vermouth on the rocks, or even a strawberry-and-basil-infused Campari and Soda. And the refreshing drinks are the perfect pair for dishes like the pane e panelle, a sandwich stacked with crispy chickpea fritters, ricotta, and caciocavallo cheese, or the heaping plate of fries topped with garlicky clams.

Website

Tavern Next Door

327 Van Brunt St, Brooklyn, NY 11231

If you’ve ever found yourself waiting for over two hours to snag a bite of Red Hook Tavern’s thick, pepper-crusted burger, we have the cocktail bar for you. The meat-slinging team recently expanded with a next-door cocktail bar that not only features one of the city’s most coveted burgers, but a whimsical cocktail menu with brightly colored creations like the tall, neon Blue Hawaiian and a refined take on an Appletini.

Website

Mash Inn

1215 8th Ave, Brooklyn, NY 11215

Located in a former laundromat in Park Slope, Mash Inn is a new bar and beer counter from the team behind Gold Star in Prospect Heights. The casual spot offers a rotating menu of beers on draft that you can enjoy in the cozy record-filled space or order growlers to-go from the beer window. The bar also offers light snacks like cheese, pickles, and charcuterie to enjoy alongside the freshly poured pints.

Website

content:
This is VinePair’s Booze News Weekly Roundup, where we gather the hottest headlines and product releases every Friday for a snapshot of what’s happening in the beverage alcohol industry. This week, we have updates on Pop-Tarts’ exit from BuzzBallz collab, Trump’s ban on Canadian alcohol, the latest product releases, and more.

News to know:

  • Pop-Tarts exits BuzzBallz partnership: Pop-Tarts’ owner Mars, Inc. backpedaled from its collaboration with popular ready-to-drink brand BuzzBallz out of fear it would target underage drinkers. Pop-Tarts cut the partnership just one month into the campaign following a meeting with the U.S. Alcohol Policy Alliance and after public health organizations co-signed a letter calling out the collab. Pop-Tarts also said it will not enter co-branded campaigns with alcohol companies in the future.
  • Trump’s ban on Canadian alcohol takes effect: President Trump’s ban on the importation of Canadian alcohol, which he threatened earlier this month after Canada enacted retaliatory tariffs on U.S. goods, took hold on Tuesday. It appears Canada won’t push back, as Prime Minister Mark Carney expects the impact of the ban, which also includes dairy and motorcycles, to be “modest,” according to BBC.
  • Strike begins at Diageo’s Cameronbridge distillery: An estimated 100 members of Unite the Union began a strike at Cameronbridge distillery — the production site for Diageo brands like Johnnie Walker, Smirnoff, and Tanqueray — this week. The union voted to walk out earlier this month after accusing the parent company of giving improper notice of job cuts at the facility. The layoffs were part of CEO Dave Lewis’ $1 billion cost-cutting, restructuring plan.
  • Black Box named official wine of NHL: The multi-year deal with E&J Gallo Winery-backed brand marks the National Hockey League’s first-ever wine partnership. As part of the collaboration, which is slated to begin in 2027, the boxed wine brand will launch programming both in arenas and across digital platforms. The heart of the deal will be Wine Wednesday programming, according to a press release, though details of the campaign have yet to be announced.
  • Google to permit alcohol advertisements on YouTube: The tech giant altered its personal advertising guidelines and will allow alcohol ads to run across YouTube beginning Oct. 30. Advertisers must still adhere to local regulations but are now able to “personalize ads on YouTube inventory for alcohol advertising, including alcohol, alcohol-related products, and alcohol alternative beverages.”

Product releases to watch:

  • Cazcanes inaugurates Experimental Single Barrel series with two releases: The brand is releasing two single-barrel reposados — one aged in ex-Mirabelle eau de vie casks and the other in ex-apricot brandy barrels, both bottled at 100 proof — to debut its new Experimental Single Barrel collection. Both reposados are now available in limited quantities for a suggested retail price of $99.99.
  • Lost Lantern releases first single-distillery bourbon: The Vermont-based bottling company is launching the George Dickel Collection, a series of bourbons all produced at the historic Cascade Hollow Distilling Co. The collection comprises 11 single-distillery and single-cask whiskies, with suggested retail prices ranging from $79.99 to $249.99.

content:
Leaning over his desk, iPhone held in the palm of his hand on speaker, 25-year-old Gavin Fernand speaks in the jargon of a stereotypical cold caller.

“Hey, how are you? I’m reaching out to see if your team has the bandwidth to support a large-scale alcohol consumption activation this afternoon?”

The unseen man on the other end of the call is a bit confused.

“Sorry, say that again?”

“We’re looking to deploy approximately 4 to 6 individuals in your establishment for a beverage-focused engagement,” adds Fernand.

Finally clueing in on the joke, the bar manager laughs and says he can accommodate them before admitting:

“That’s the best call we’ve gotten all day.”

Fernand is part of a growing wave of young people dialing up bars on camera — some to prank, some to “check the vibe,” most just to see what happens. For a generation that supposedly neither drinks nor speaks on the phone, it’s an unlikely viral trend.

Going in Cold

Posting under the handle Corporate Dudes, Fernand runs a consulting company that makes skits, funny videos, and memes paid for by alcohol brands like Guinness, Surfside, and Shock Top as well as non-drinks companies like Adobe and Ramp. But he also creates his own funny drinks content for his social media business which counts 2 million followers across 7 accounts.

Fernand found early success this year with a series called Lunch Beer, in which he stops a stranger on the street in the middle of the work day and brings them out to a bar to have a drink and chew the fat. Calling bars to try and get permission to film there, he came up with his next big idea.

One day, a co-worker was taking his “sweet-ass time” to wrap for the day and so Fernand thought it would be funny to call their local bar to tell them they were going to be “a little late” for their usual happy hour perch. That video went semi-viral, with around 14,000 likes and 5,000 shares on TikTok; Fernand was inspired to do more. He was already skilled at cold-calling random people (and its jargony argot) thanks to a former gig as an SDR (sales development representative) which saw him cold calling sometimes 200 people a day.

“There had been trends of people like cold-calling their girlfriend or something like that, so I thought I could take that and spin it into this different niche,” says Fernand.

It worked, and his bar cold-call video has over 200,000 likes so far.

Pranking the Bar

Prank calls to bars are of course nothing new — see: Bart Simpson’s calls to Moe’s Tavern which was based on the cult-famous Tube Bar tapes from the 1970s — but, in many ways, this trend comes on the heels of a similar trend that started in late 2024, when social media users began calling bars to simply “check the vibe.”

One of the earliest TikToks of a Zoomer cold-calling the bar doesn’t even post the actual phone call. Instead, musician Fia James recounts a story of her and a friend calling a bar to check the vibes — “Are there any cuties?” they ask — stunning a bartender who’d apparently never considered that this was something people could do. Honestly, even though James is pretty charming, the video is not all that entertaining; nevertheless, it racked up nearly three-quarters of a million views and soon had copycats.

By March 2025, TikToker Bethany Kelly had gone viral for calling a Cincinnati bar on St. Patrick’s day to see what the vibes are and whether people are wearing green and it’s “giving St. Patrick’s Day.” The bartender earnestly responds to all her queries and the video eventually received 5 million views.

“With these videos, we’re trying to highlight the benefits of social interaction, getting out there and meeting people, making friends with strangers even just for a night, and why that is, like, so important.”

A week later, pre-hangover pear drink brand Gush went viral with a video in which a woman calls a bar “to see what the vibes are.” “Uh…what?!” responded the bartender before he claimed (falsely it sure sounds like) that the bar was packed with a solid male/female ratio. It received nearly 6 million views on TikTok.

This would soon spread across the world, with cold-calling vibe checkers in Ireland (“Is there any good craic in the pub?”) and other countries. This trend has continued to the present day and now TikTok has an entire page dedicated to “Normalize Calling The Bar to Check The Vibe.”

Last Call

Generation Z famously does not make phone calls and we’ve long been told they don’t drink alcohol either — though new data suggests the latter is more stereotype than fact.

Yet, Fernand does both and so now do plenty of other Zoomers. Calling bars (and hopefully then drinking at them) is just something you do if you’re a young person with a social media account and a desire for virality. For Fernand, it’s not just a laugh, but a little life lesson.

“Comfortability is like the edge for me, myself, and people I know in sales,” says Fernand. “I think being able to call someone and just speak normally and be humble enough to admit that you don’t know the answer if they ask something — it’s a good skill to have, you know.”

Perhaps that’s why calling bars has caught on so quickly. There are people calling bars to let them know they are now hungover (“I came into your establishment yesterday and had a few beers…”). There are people calling to see if the bar knows what happened last night (“I was there for my 21st birthday last night and I’m really not feeling good…”). Others are calling the bar to wish them goodnight. It’s even extended to college buddies cold-calling each other to try to tempt them into going out drinking for the night (“Sounds tempting…”).

Of course, likes and shares aren’t bar traffic, but, ultimately, through his videos and this trend, Fernand believes he is showing that his generation is being incorrectly perceived as lame and boring.

“That’s a stigma we’re trying to beat,” he says. “With these videos, we’re trying to highlight the benefits of social interaction, getting out there and meeting people, making friends with strangers even just for a night, and why that is, like, so important.”

Just last week, while on vacation, Fernand called his local Murray Hill dive Buddy’s to let them know he’s “OK” and will be back in town (and at their bar) soon. The bar manager’s response:

“I appreciate the call and I’ll let the staff know you’re in good hands.”
